newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbia Parliament mulls new privatisation law.
newsitem.headline: Serbia Parliament mulls new privatisation law.

text.p: Serbia's parliament is discussing a landmark privatisation bill whose quick adoption would pave the way for a market economy and set up the ownership structure in almost 5,000 medium and small companies.
"With the ownership transformation law, Serbia's government is rounding up years of activity aimed at creating a modern market econmy," Serbian Prime Minister Mirko Marjanovic told the parliament.
Marjanovic insisted the bill, the first of its kind in half a century of leftist rule, was a part of comprehensive reforms.
"Today.. with $1,600 per capita income, high growth rate and with price and dinar stability we are completely ready to transform our economy in full," he said.
Serbia's economy has been devastated by 3 1/2 years of sanctions, which were lifted in 1995, the collapse of the former Yugoslav market, mismanagement, and wars in Bosnia and Croatia.

Serbia is still barred from foreign funds and world financial institutions like the International Montenery Fund by an outer wall of sanctions which Washington has promised to dismantle only after Belgrade meets several democracy-related conditions.

Serbian authorities have resorted to privatising major assets like its telecommunications service which was recently sold to Italian and Greek telecom monopolies in order to obtain the hard currency needed to restart its economy.

"The law creates a new economic civilisation... a new environment, management structure, good motivation for foreign investments, improved allocation of resources, strengthens competition and breaks monopolies," Serbian Privatisation Minister Milan Beko said.
The minister insisted privatisation, even though not compulsory, would be inevitable. He said the state was there to create a legal framework within which market mechanisms will be set free.

"It is important to enter the privatisation process, someone will always earn something but these funds must start circulating in Serbia," said Tomislav Nikolic, vice-president of the Serbian Raadical Party.
No amendments have been submitted and the bill is expected to be passed later in the day.
Main objections to the law expressed by some experts are on transparency, fairness and why the unemployed were not included in the process.
